title: Materialised symmetries of 2D translationally invariant codes
authors: Andrew Li, Stephen D. Bartlett, Andrew C. Doherty, Campbell K. McLauchlan
abstract: There has been significant recent interest in near-term qLDPC codes as high-performance alternatives to surface and color codes. One such class of codes is 2-dimensional translationally invariant (TI) codes, such as bivariate bicycle codes, which share similar properties to topological codes. Fundamental objects in the study of such codes are the materialised symmetries, which can be used for the construction of matching-based decoders. These decoders generalise the minimum-weight perfect matching decoder for toric codes and provide similar asymptotic performance guarantees that heuristic decoders such as BP and its variants lack. Despite this, the mathematical structure of symmetries along with their properties under translation and restriction to finite-sized lattices has not been well-studied. We describe a decomposition of symmetry spaces of 2D CSS TI codes on infinite lattices into translation-invariant subspaces which allow us to write an explicit basis of symmetries in a plane-wave-like form. We then describe how to adapt this infinite lattice basis so that any corresponding rectangular periodic lattice basis can be obtained by restriction to basis elements compatible with the periodic boundaries. This allows us to describe how the symmetry space varies with different rectangular dimensions. We illustrate via examples that it is often straightforward in practice to determine a basis of symmetries on twisted boundaries as well, without needing to recompute the decomposition. We comment on the applications of this framework to matching-based decoders and provide examples of symmetries of such codes as the gross code.
summary: This paper provides a comprehensive mathematical framework for characterizing the symmetries of 2D translationally invariant quantum error-correcting codes. By decomposing the symmetry space into translation-invariant subspaces, the authors offer a systematic way to determine how these symmetries behave across different finite boundary conditions. This work is crucial for advancing the design and performance analysis of matching-based quantum decoders.
main_problem: The paper aims to rigorously study the mathematical structure and properties of 'materialised symmetries' within 2D translationally invariant (TI) quantum error-correcting codes.
main_result: The authors develop a framework to decompose the symmetry space into translation-invariant subspaces, providing an explicit, plane-wave-like basis that can be adapted to arbitrary rectangular periodic lattices and even twisted boundaries.
method: The methodology involves analyzing the code structure using the language of CSS chain complexes over Laurent polynomials, relating symmetries to dual modules, and employing techniques from algebraic topology and module theory.
model_or_system: The focus is on 2D translationally invariant quantum error-correcting codes (e.g., bivariate bicycle and color codes) defined on an infinite lattice, analyzed using Haah's formalism.
key_observables: Materialised symmetries, metachecks (subsets of stabilizer checks multiplying to identity), and the decomposition of the symmetry space into irreducible periodic components.
important_parameters: The lattice dimensions (rectangular periodicity) and the underlying algebraic structure defined by the code generators (A and B).
main_assumptions: The analysis heavily relies on the assumption that the code structure can be modeled by an exact CSS chain complex over the ring of Laurent polynomials.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the cyclic translation of X or Z symmetries for the hexagonal color code, demonstrating translational periodicity.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the algebraic framework using Laurent polynomials, deriving the decomposition of the symmetry space, showing how this infinite basis restricts to finite periodic lattices, and finally discussing extensions to twisted boundaries and applications to matching-based decoders.
why_interesting: The deep algebraic understanding of symmetries in these codes provides powerful tools for designing and analyzing quantum error correction codes, which is central to fault-tolerant quantum computation.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. The rg, gb, and br X or Z symmetries of the hexagonal color code. The arrow is a translation that cycles between symmetries.

FIG. 2. Schematic illustration of the decomposition of R′/J. Each component corresponds to polynomial functions at a point (αi, βi), but fat points (i = 2, 3) include additional structure in their neighbourhood. The points occur at the intersection of A = 0 (black) and B = 0 (blue).

FIG. 3. A patch of color code on a planar lattice, as described by the polynomials A = 1 + x + xy, B = 1 + y + xy. Note how each color of check lives along sets of diagonals (i, j) ≡c (mod 3) with c = 0 for red, c = 1 for green, and c = 2 for blue.

FIG. 4. Computing symmetries of the gross code on 6 × 12 boundaries. (Left) The (ω, ω)-component of the gross code K-symmetries is spanned by {δ1} (blue). This fits in any non-zero box. (Right) The (ω, ω2)-component of the gross code K-symmetries is spanned by {δ1, δv + ωδu, δv2 + ω2δu2} (blue, green, and pink respectively). The pink basis element does not fit inside the box.

FIG. 5. Adapting a basis for rectangular boundaries. (Left) An example of a basis {u2v2 +u3v2 +u4v2, u2 +u3v +u4v2} where neither basis element (highlighted in pink and blue respectively) survives intersection with B, but their sum does. (Right) An ‘adapted’ basis of the same subspace where upon intersection with B, the blue basis element survives and the pink does not. The blue basis element spans the subspace after intersection.
